title: Scheduled Task/Job
summary: Scheduled task abuse is the practice of registering work with the operating system's own scheduler so that attacker code runs at a chosen time, at start-up, or repeatedly without further interaction. Every mainstream platform ships such a service: the Windows Task Scheduler driven by schtasks, the task XML store and the Task Scheduler service; the cron daemon on Unix-like systems reading per-user crontab files and system directories; systemd timers on modern Linux; and orchestration job objects such as Kubernetes CronJobs. The mechanism matters defensively because the scheduler is a trusted component. It launches the payload as its own child process, often under a privileged account, so parent process and signature checks alone no longer explain the execution. The record left behind is configuration as much as runtime: task definitions on disk or in a database, creation and registration events in the scheduler's own log, and the resulting process creation events at each run. Legitimate software uses exactly the same interfaces, so the differentiators are the command line and its arguments, the account context, the triggering schedule, the directory the payload runs from, and whether the same binary is also launched interactively.

beginner.definition: Every operating system can run a program for you at a chosen time. It works like an alarm clock that wakes you each morning. This technique is when an attacker uses that built-in clock to run their own code. It is not a bug in the clock, because the clock is doing exactly what it was asked to do. The attacker simply gives it instructions that the owner never intended.
beginner.whyItMatters: If malicious code runs on a schedule, it comes back after you clean it up. It can also run as a powerful account that you do not control, which makes the damage worse. Security tools often trust the scheduler, so the code looks like a normal system event. Understanding which schedulers exist lets you look in the right places for the attacker's instructions.
howItWorks: The attacker gains the ability to run commands on a machine, often with a normal user account at first.
They create a scheduled entry that points to a program, script or document on the disk.
They choose a trigger, such as a fixed time each day, a delay, a logon, or system start-up.
They may also choose which account the entry runs as, hoping for a more powerful one.
The scheduler starts the program when the trigger fires, so the code runs with no attacker present.
If the entry is removed, the code stops, so attackers also try to hide the entry itself.
beginner.example: Think of an office building with a key card system. A contractor asks the front desk for a door code that works every Tuesday at six in the morning. The code is legitimate and the system approves it, because the request form was filled in correctly. Nobody questions why a cleaner needs the server room at that hour. The cleaner arrives, does something nobody expects, and leaves before staff arrive.
takeaways: Scheduled tasks make malicious code survive restarts and clean-up attempts.
The thing to review is the instruction, not only the process that runs it.
Each platform has its own scheduler, so your checks must cover all of them.

objectives: Name the scheduling mechanism used on Windows, on Linux and inside container clusters.
Explain how a scheduler turns a saved instruction into repeated code execution.
Describe why scheduler-driven execution is harder to explain from process trees alone.
Identify the configuration artefacts and event records a new scheduled job creates.
Compare a suspicious scheduled entry with a legitimate one using command line, account and timing.
